children: State-run oil marketing companies seek 11 billion litres of ethanol from grain-based feedstocks, while reducing the price incentive for corn-based supplies

India has set sugar diversion for ethanol production at zero for the 2026-27 supply year, excluding sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses from the latest procurement tender. The move comes amid concerns over domestic sugar availability, lower production prospects and rising prices.

The tender, issued on 16 October by Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation, invites bids for 11 billion litres of ethanol for the supply year beginning in November. Suppliers can offer ethanol made from corn, broken rice and surplus rice procured by the Food Corporation of India.
The decision signals a shift in feedstock procurement as India seeks to balance its ethanol-blending programme with the need to maintain domestic sugar supplies.

The tender states that the government has directed oil marketing companies to reduce sugar diversion for ethanol production to zero for the 2026-27 supply year. Accordingly, the companies have not invited bids for ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar or sugar syrup, and B-heavy molasses.

India has used surplus sugar and sugarcane-based feedstocks to support ethanol production and reduce dependence on imported crude oil. The latest tender instead directs procurement towards grain-based alternatives, including corn and rice.

The change comes as poor rainfall in key sugar-producing states, including Maharashtra and Karnataka, has raised concerns about sugar output. Lower production prospects have added pressure to domestic supplies and prices.
The tender also reduces the incentive for corn-based ethanol to Rs 2.79 per litre from Rs 5.79 per litre. The procurement price consequently falls to Rs 68.86 per litre from Rs 71.86 per litre.

The lower incentive changes the commercial terms for suppliers that use corn as a feedstock. The impact on procurement and production will depend on the economics of grain availability, processing costs and the prices offered under the tender.

The procurement framework allows suppliers to use surplus rice procured by the Food Corporation of India, alongside corn and broken rice. This provides alternative feedstocks as sugar-based ethanol remains outside the latest tender.

India has expanded ethanol blending to reduce crude oil imports and curb pollution. The government made the E20 blend, which contains 20 per cent ethanol, the nationwide mandatory standard earlier in 2026. However, some motorists have raised concerns about its compatibility with older vehicles.
